title: The Hallway Clock
statement: A hallway clock gains time at a constant rate. Earlier in the day, it showed exactly the correct time. When the correct time was $14:00$, the clock showed $14:06$. When the correct time was $16:00$, the clock showed $16:10$. How many minutes before the correct time of $14:00$ did the clock show exactly the correct time?
hints: Don't track the clock's readings themselves. Instead, work out how many minutes ahead of the correct time the clock is at $14:00$ and at $16:00$.

Treat the clock's lead as a quantity that changes at a constant rate. The clock is $6$ minutes ahead at $14:00$ and $10$ minutes ahead at $16:00$, so find how many true minutes it takes to gain $1$ minute.

The lead grows by $4$ minutes during the $120$ true minutes from $14:00$ to $16:00$, so the clock gains $1$ minute every $30$ true minutes. Now work backwards from $14:00$ to the moment when the lead was $0$.
solution: Call the number of minutes by which the clock is ahead of the correct time its lead. The lead is $6$ minutes at $14:00$ and $10$ minutes at $16:00$. Since the clock gains time at a constant rate, its lead changes by equal amounts in equal periods of true time. From $14:00$ to $16:00$, the lead grows by $10 - 6 = 4$ minutes in $120$ true minutes. So the clock gains $1$ minute every $\frac{120}{4} = 30$ true minutes. The clock showed the correct time exactly when its lead was $0$. Its lead then grew at this same rate to reach $6$ minutes at $14:00$, which took $6 \cdot 30 = 180$ true minutes. The answer is $180$. Why this works. rate-and-mixture-modeling, reverse-the-process: the clock's lead grows at a constant rate, so that rate can be run backwards from $14:00$ to the moment the lead was zero.
